name: Kuduro
notes: Kuduro style pack (Doc 04 template, solo-first). Luanda's hard-edged electronic street dance, with a creator credited by name and one of dance history's best origin stories: TONY AMADO created kuduro in late-1980s Luanda — by his own famous account, after watching Jean-Claude Van Damme dance stiff and drunk in the film Kickboxer, he set that rigid, hard-hipped movement to Angolan electronic beats and named it KUDURO — 'hard ass' in Angolan Portuguese slang — for exactly how it moves. SEBEM pioneered the animador vocal style that made it a genre. The honesty this pack holds: kuduro grew up during ANGOLA'S CIVIL WAR (1975–2002), danced in Luanda's musseques (informal neighborhoods) as youth resilience — celebration with shrapnel in its biography, and famously a dance where disabled dancers, including war-injured performers, built visible careers on crutches and prosthetics: kuduro's aesthetic of jolts, drops, and improvised angles made room for every body the war sent home. The Lisbon diaspora carried it to Europe, and BURAKA SOM SISTEMA wired it into global club music in the 2000s. The batida rides in this app's Rhythm Trainer. Safety is structural: the drops and floor hits are knee-gated and progressive.

seasons.finale: Film yourself locking to the batida for one track — hard hits on the grid, loose recovery between them.
Film the hard-hip basic — Van Damme rigidity on the hits, total looseness between — one full song.
Film the fast-feet patterns at three speeds — the last one just past comfortable.
Film a drop run: three level drops with clean returns, knees warmed, landings soft, angles ugly on purpose.
Take kuduro to a floor — an African or Lusophone club night, a kuduro battle circle — and bring the hardness with the joy.

attributes.name: Drop-ready knees L2
attributes.test: 10 controlled squat-drops to low level with soft catches and immediate returns, no pain — the floor moves are earned, not survived

attributes.name: Hit-and-release core L1
attributes.test: 60s alternating between a hard full-body tension hit and instant looseness on a beat — the contrast IS the style

attributes.name: Batida stamina L2
attributes.test: two tracks at 140bpm of continuous work — kuduro runs hot and does not idle

nodes.name: The batida — 140 and merciless
checkpoints: kuduro rides the BATIDA — a hard electronic 4/4 around 140bpm with syncopated snare jabs; it's in this app's Rhythm Trainer
the animador (the track's shouting MC — Sebem made the role) calls the energy and the moves, cousin to Kinshasa's atalaku and Abidjan's hype-callers
train the grid first: kuduro's hits land ON the beat with machine precision — the looseness lives between the hits, never on them

nodes.name: Luanda → Lisbon → the world
checkpoints: the Angolan diaspora carried kuduro to Lisbon's periphery, where a second scene grew — and BURAKA SOM SISTEMA wired the batida into global club music in the 2000s ('Sound of Kuduro' put it on the world's speakers)
the credit direction matters: Lisbon amplified what Luanda invented — say it in that order
today's playlist spans both shores: classic Luanda kuduro, Lisbon batida producers, and the Angolan stars who never needed the detour

nodes.name: Tony Amado — the creator and the Van Damme story
checkpoints: kuduro was CREATED by TONY AMADO in late-1980s Luanda — by his own famous telling, after watching Jean-Claude Van Damme dance stiff and drunk in Kickboxer, he set that rigid movement to Angolan electronic beats
he named it KUDURO — 'hard ass' — for exactly how it moves: locked hips, hard hits, zero apology; SEBEM pioneered the animador vocals that made it a genre
a named creator, a dated origin, a story with a movie in it — credit Tony Amado every time someone calls street dance 'anonymous folk culture'

nodes.name: The musseques — resilience with shrapnel in it
checkpoints: kuduro grew up during Angola's civil war (1975–2002), danced in Luanda's musseques as youth resilience — celebration with shrapnel in its biography, the same decision Abidjan made with coupé-décalé

kuduro made room for every body the war sent home: disabled and war-injured dancers built visible, celebrated careers in it — the style's jolts and improvised angles welcome bodies other dances exclude
hold both truths when you dance it: the joy is real AND it was expensive — kuduro danced as empty aerobics erases its receipt

nodes.name: The animador — Sebem's role
checkpoints: the ANIMADOR is kuduro's voice: shouted commands, catchphrases, and crowd-work riding the batida — SEBEM pioneered the role and turned kuduro from a beat into a genre
the animador names moves and the floor executes — same steering-wheel job as Kinshasa's atalaku, evolved independently on the same continent-wide instinct
train responsiveness: dance a track and change SOMETHING within one bar of every vocal shout — command-latency is a kuduro skill

nodes.name: The hard-hip basic — stiff on purpose
checkpoints: the signature: hips locked HARD, a rigid full-body hit landing on the beat — then instant looseness between hits; the contrast is the whole aesthetic
think Van Damme's drunk stagger made precise: stiff, angular, deliberately awkward shapes executed with total control
the hits are percussive — a viewer should be able to hear the batida by watching your body with the sound off
mistakes: staying tense between hits (the release sells the hit — permanent stiffness is just being stiff)
prettifying the angles (kuduro's shapes are ugly on purpose; elegance is a different pack)

nodes.name: Fast feet
checkpoints: rapid small-step patterns under the locked torso — shuffles, stamps, and crossing steps chattering at batida speed
three-speed drill: half-time until clean, on-tempo until comfortable, then push past comfortable for one chorus
the feet are busy so the torso can be stubborn — the layers must not leak into each other

nodes.name: Drops & floor hits
checkpoints: sudden level drops — squat catches, knee dips, controlled falls to the floor and back up inside one bar
progression is law: half-depth drops for a week before full, soft surfaces before hard, warm knees always
the return is the move: hitting the floor is gravity's work; being back on the batida's next ONE is yours
mistakes: dropping cold or on concrete first (the knee attribute is a gate, not a suggestion)

nodes.name: Jolts, tremors & broken angles
checkpoints: kuduro's texture layer: electric jolts through one limb, full-body tremors, joints bent to deliberately broken-looking angles and held
asymmetry is welcome by design — one arm working against a dead-still other is more kuduro than symmetry ever is
improvise angles the mirror finds strange; if it looks almost wrong, it's almost right

nodes.name: The musseque set — filmed
checkpoints: film one full track: stiff basic hitting the grid, fast feet under it, two drops with clean returns, jolts texturing the gaps
sound-off review: can a viewer reconstruct the batida from your body alone? that's the pass condition
say the credits on camera: Tony Amado, Luanda, 'hard ass' — the name is the history

nodes.name: The battle floor
checkpoints: find it live: Lusophone and African club nights, kuduro battle circles, and Lisbon's batida parties run worldwide
kuduro floors read commitment, not polish — enter hard, keep the angles honest, leave everything on the batida
afterward, tell one person the Van Damme story; it's the best gateway drug dance history owns
